questions.knowledge_point: Solving an Initial Value Problem: Purely Imaginary Eigenvalues
questions.problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

*Hint: One of the eigenvalues of the matrix is ${\lambda }_{1}=\text{i}.$*
questions.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}].$

We are given that the eigenvalue is ${\lambda }_{1}=\text{i}.$ 

Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors. For ${\lambda }_{1}=\text{i},$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} & -1 \\ 1 & -\text{i}\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\text{i} \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{\text{i}t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{\text{i}t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}](\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & =-[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 5 & 4\end{aligned}]x(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

*Hint: The matrix has the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=2+\text{i}$ with the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2+\text{i} \\ 5\end{aligned}].$*
questions.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 5 & 4\end{aligned}].$ 

We are given the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=2+\text{i}$ and the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2+\text{i} \\ 5\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=2+\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-2+\text{i} \\ 5\end{aligned}]{e}^{(2+\text{i})t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}-2+\text{i} \\ 5\end{aligned}]{e}^{(2+\text{i})t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2+\text{i} \\ 5\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2{e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}(-2{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\text{i}({e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 5{e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}(5{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2{e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\text{i}({e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\ 5{e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}(5{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t} \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 5\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2{c}_{1}+{c}_{2} \\ 5{c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{5} \\ -\frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & =\frac{3}{5}[\begin{aligned}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}-\frac{4}{5}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡t-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -16 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

*Hint: One of the eigenvalues of the matrix is ${\lambda }_{1}=4\text{i}.$*
questions.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -16 & 0\end{aligned}].$

We are given that the eigenvalue is ${\lambda }_{1}=4\text{i}.$ 

Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors. For ${\lambda }_{1}=4\text{i},$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=[\begin{aligned}-4\text{i} & 1 \\ -16 & -4\text{i}\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}4 & \text{i} \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}\text{i} \\ -4\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=4\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}\text{i} \\ -4\end{aligned}]{e}^{4\text{i}t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}\text{i} \\ -4\end{aligned}]{e}^{4\text{i}t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\text{i} \\ -4\end{aligned}](\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\text{i}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ -4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-4\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+\text{i}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\ -4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-4\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ -4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}]+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\ -4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}] \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ -4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\ -4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -4\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} \\ -4{c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & =0[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ -4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\ -4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\ -8\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 10 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above.
Find the unknown function $f(t)$ in the general solution to the system, shown below.

$$
\text{x}(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ f(t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}
$$

*Hint: The matrix has the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=2+3\text{i}$ with the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1-3\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$*
questions.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 10 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}].$ 

We are given the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=2+3\text{i}$ and the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1-3\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=2+3\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}1-3\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(2+3\text{i})t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}1-3\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(2+3\text{i})t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1-3\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-3\text{i}{e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+3{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ {e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))+\text{i}{e}^{2t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)) \\ {e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t} \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $f(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).$

questions.problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -5 \\ 1 & -6\end{aligned}]x(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

*Hint: The matrix has the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-4+\text{i}$ with the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2+\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$*
questions.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -5 \\ 1 & -6\end{aligned}].$ 

We are given the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-4+\text{i}$ and the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2+\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-4+\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2+\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(-4+\text{i})t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}2+\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(-4+\text{i})t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2+\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-4t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{-4t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\text{i}{e}^{-4t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\text{i}{e}^{-4t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{-4t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ {e}^{-4t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}{e}^{-4t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{-4t}+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{-4t} \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{-4t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{-4t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2{c}_{1}+{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & =-[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{-4t}+3[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{-4t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{-4t}.\end{aligned}
$$
